problems: PROMPT/ARTIFACT MISMATCH (not a page defect): the task prompt's 'Claimed scenario' and 'Claimed mechanism' describe a DIFFERENT page than the file on disk. Prompt claims classList.remove('hide') vs .hidden{display:none}, an aria-describedby='pw-rules' resolving to a hidden node, an element #pw-rules, and 'on focus the field shows only empty space'. The actual file has NONE of these: no #pw-rules element (confirmed pwRulesElExists=false), no '.hidden' CSS rule (anyHideClassCSS=false), no remove('hide') anywhere, no aria-describedby on #pw (pwDescribedby=null), and on focus the field does NOT show empty space — it reveals the EMAIL hint (#email-hint -> display:block, class 'hint show'). The actual bug is a copy-paste wrong-target-id: the #pw focus handler (HTML lines 132-137) calls document.getElementById('email-hint').classList.add('show') instead of 'pw-hint'. My verdict is based on the real HTML+MD, which are internally consistent and correct.

Minor: this case shares the 'focus-revealed instruction not honored' aspect with sibling cases; confirm corpus-level distinctness so it is not a near-duplicate of another case in the same folder (the wrong-target-id variant is distinct from a missing/no-op handler variant, so this is likely fine).

Doc mechanism OVERSTATES the screen-reader impact: .md lines 38-41 and HTML comment lines 20-21 claim screen-reader users never receive the instruction, but the AX tree shows #promo carries description='Format: three letters, a dash, then four digits — for example ABC-1234.' via aria-describedby, independent of the CSS collapse. SR users DO get it on focus; the real failing population is keyboard-only SIGHTED users.
The failure should be scoped to the VISIBLE-instruction-on-focus limb (TT 5.A), not the programmatic association — the aria-describedby IS surfaced to AT.

Minor scope nuance (not a defect): the AX tree shows the #travel textbox exposes the format hint as an accessible description via aria-describedby="travel-hint" (description='Use day-first format DD/MM/YYYY ...'). A screen-reader user therefore DOES receive the instruction; the failure is correctly limited to sighted-keyboard / low-vision / magnifier users. The .md doc states this honestly, so it narrows but does not invalidate the failed outcome.

Minor accuracy caveat in the .md/mechanism: the doc claims 'a screen reader re-querying the description finds nothing' after the timeout, but the Chromium CDP AX snapshot at ~2s (focus retained) STILL reports the input's description text ('Usernames are 3-20 characters...'). This is because Chromium computes aria-describedby text by traversing the referenced node's subtree even when that node is aria-hidden=true and opacity:0. The load-bearing barrier is therefore the VISUAL/perceivable disappearance (opacity:0) for sighted-slow, low-vision, and magnifier users (which the doc correctly leads with); the specific SR-finds-nothing claim is implementation-dependent and not borne out by this AX snapshot. Does not change the failed verdict.

Minor self-containment note: the tooltip node is opacity:0 (not display:none) before focus and is reachable in the AX tree at the initial static snapshot, so the instruction text is exposed pre-focus to a static scan — consistent with the doc's 'automated tools miss it' framing, but worth noting the pre-focus state is visually hidden yet AX-present.

No genuine defect — this is a deliberate PASSING boundary variant and the 'passed' label is correct (errorIsReal=true means the documented condition genuinely holds: there is NO real accessibility error, as intended).

Minor doc imprecision: the .md/HTML comment claims '140 meaningful characters' but the hint's visible text is 169 chars when measured (full textContent). top=354 matches my measurement. Not material — the text is unambiguously real and meaningful.

Nuance (not a defect): the aria-describedby='policy-hint' description is exposed in the AX tree even in the RESTING (display:none) state (inspect.js shows description on the unfocused textbox). 3.3.2 / TT 5.A is about the VISIBLE instruction, which is correctly focus-gated, so this does not undermine the pass; it would only matter if the SC under test were the programmatic association (1.3.1/4.1.2).

Outcome label rests on a contested SC boundary: the NORMATIVE 3.3.2 text + the Trusted Tester procedure (Test 5.A, which the doc itself quotes from refs/trusted-tester/sc-3.3.2-labels-or-instructions.md:28 'this test only determines whether visual labels/instructions are present, regardless of accuracy') would mark this field PASS, because an instruction IS provided and correctly associated (AX tree confirms #dob description='Format: MM/DD/YYYY — for example 03/27/1986'). The 'failed' verdict is defensible only under a PURPOSIVE/Intent reading. A reasonable reviewer could argue a wrong instruction is more naturally a 3.3.1/3.3.3 concern (error identification/suggestion) than a 3.3.2 failure. The doc is transparent about this tension, so it is a caveat, not a fabrication.

The case label/selector says #dob-hint but the actual a11y failure surface is the #dob field whose enforced rule (pattern + JS DDMMYYYY regex) contradicts the hint — the hint element in isolation is benign; the defect is the hint-vs-pattern relationship. Selector choice is acceptable (the misleading text lives in #dob-hint) but slightly understates that the contradiction is the unit under test.

Minor (not a defect): the element-under-test selector #otp-help has ax.name="" because it is a paragraph whose text is consumed as the group's accessible name via aria-labelledby. The defect lives in the helper-prose-vs-field-rule mismatch, not in the selector node itself; this is correct but could confuse a reviewer who expects the named element to carry the name.

SCOPE-ATTRIBUTION TENSION (does not invalidate the case, but worth recording): the cited Understanding doc itself states (wcag-understanding/labels-or-instructions.html lines 64-67) that 'whether or not labels (if used) are accurate, sufficiently clear, or descriptive is covered separately by 2.4.6 Headings and Labels,' and lines 48-53 push correct markup to 1.3.1. 3.3.2 is fundamentally a PRESENCE criterion. The instruction IS present, associated, perceivable, and names the specific input rules. A present-but-numerically-stale value ('8' vs enforced 12) is arguably 2.4.6/3.3.1 territory. The 'failed' verdict relies on the broader Intent reading (instructions must 'specify rules for correct input' so users 'enter information correctly') — defensible but contestable; this is the human-judgment crux of the case.

The page's own .md citation (line 37-38, refs/trusted-tester Test 5.A note) explicitly says the procedure determines presence 'regardless of accuracy' — this candidly undercuts a strict-letter 3.3.2 failure and reinforces that the failed label depends on a purposive (not procedural) reading.

Minor (non-blocking): the primary WCAG citation describes a THREE-field phone control with legend 'Phone number', while this page implements a FOUR-field control (added country code) with legend 'Phone number (US, 10 digits)'. The quote is verbatim (understanding doc lines 128-129) and correctly establishes the sanctioned H71 group-instruction pattern, so it still supports the claim; just note the example is not a 1:1 structural match to the page.

Minor SC-boundary nuance (not a defect): the failure also has Error Prevention/Error Suggestion adjacency, but it sits squarely within 3.3.2's 'examples of expected data formats' benefit, so the 3.3.2 mapping is defensible.

Partial automated-detectability caveat (does not change verdict): an HTML form validator would reject a user-entered '25.00' against pattern=\d+, but no automated tool reads the literal '25.00' out of the instruction PROSE and tests it against the field rule — the prose-vs-constraint contradiction is the genuinely human-judgment part.

SC-boundary tension (the only real weakness): the case frames the failure as the instruction being INACCURATE (names wrong purpose), but the cited WCAG Understanding doc itself states at lines 64-67 'whether or not labels (if used) are accurate, sufficiently clear, or descriptive is covered separately by 2.4.6 Headings and Labels' — and the TT ref scope note (refs/trusted-tester/sc-3.3.2-labels-or-instructions.md:33) says '3.3.2 in TT is strictly is-a-visible-label-present; Adequacy is 2.4.6'. The doc does not acknowledge this overlap. The 3.3.2 attribution is defensible because the instruction misstates the DATA-ENTRY RULE/expected input (8 digits) — which falls under 3.3.2's explicit 'specify data formats... specific rules for correct input' (Understanding lines 29-31) and 'know what input data is expected' intent — rather than merely being un-descriptive. But it is genuinely arguable and sits on the 3.3.2/2.4.6 boundary; reviewers could reasonably classify it as 2.4.6.

Minor: doc lists three citation blocks; the third (TT 5.A 'present, regardless of accuracy') is accurate but slightly undercuts the 3.3.2 framing since it foregrounds that accuracy is out of TT 5.A's reach.

Minor interpretive nuance (not a defect): SC 3.3.2 is sometimes read leniently as satisfied once any label identifies the control. The 'visible-cue-adequacy' / 'widely-understood image' limb invoked here is an interpretive stance rather than a hard ACT rule with a stable rule ID. It is, however, explicitly anticipated by the WCAG Understanding text (lines 43-46 on widely-understood image labels; lines 54-59 on passing 4.1.2 via aria-label but still failing 3.3.2 when labels aren't presented to all users), so the 'failed' verdict is well-supported and citation-backed.

Outcome is genuinely borderline (defensible, not slam-dunk): a strict reading of 3.3.2 treats the SC as satisfied once any visible cue is present; the 'images must be widely understood' requirement lives in the non-normative Understanding text, so a reviewer could rate this 'passed'. The page leans on the audience-relative 'widely understood' judgment, which is exactly the intended human-judgment hook but keeps severity minor.

The visible '/ 10' suffix plus an adjustment-style glyph arguably conveys 'a 1-10 scale of some adjustable setting', weakening (but not refuting) the claim that a sighted user gets zero meaningful cue.

Visible on-page developer 'devnote' meta-commentary (lines 90-96) leaks the test's intent into the rendered page and the AX tree (StaticText nodes 44-48); cosmetically un-naturalistic but does not affect the verdict.

SC mapping is contestable (minor, not disqualifying): the clock IS a visible cue, so a reviewer could argue this is a 2.4.6 'inaccurate/unclear label' issue rather than a 3.3.2 failure. The Understanding doc explicitly routes whether labels are 'accurate, sufficiently clear, or descriptive' to 2.4.6 (lines 64-67 of wcag-understanding/labels-or-instructions.html). The page's 3.3.2 reading is defensible via the image-label 'widely understood by the intended target audience' limb (lines 43-46), but it is not the only reasonable SC. The underlying barrier is unambiguous; only the SC label is dual-citable.

None that undermine the verdict. 1Attendee 1
; inspect.js selector text => '1Attendee 1'; AX tree contains StaticText 'Attendee 1' and StaticText 'Attendee 2'. So the prompt's core premise is refuted by the source and by Chromium's AX tree.

The file's OWN .md mechanism (real-but-orphaned chrome, F82-generalized) is internally consistent and AX-corroborated (both blocks expose byte-identical names: textbox 'Full name', textbox 'Email for the ticket', combobox 'T-shirt size'; sections carry no accessible name), BUT it is borderline as a 3.3.2 FAILURE: the 'Attendee 1/2' text is real StaticText in document order immediately preceding each group, so a browse-mode SR user DOES encounter it. The 'failed' verdict rests entirely on a contestable pure-forms-mode AT-behavior assumption; many ACT auditors would treat per-control labels-present + adjacent on-screen group text as passed/advisory, not a clear failure.

Net: errorIsReal=false because the prompt's stated mechanism does not exist in this file; expectedOutcomeCorrect=false because the prompt's scenario/mechanism/selector/citation-framing (CSS-generated content) is wrong for the artifact and the residual file-own mechanism is weaker/arguable than 'failed'.

Mechanism imprecision (not outcome-affecting): the doc/HTML comment claim the SR user hears 'Current address, Street address, edit' via aria-labelledby. The Chromium AX tree shows the textbox accessible names are ONLY the inner labels ('Street address','City','State','ZIP', lines 178-181/244-247/etc.); the group name lives on the parent role=region node (name 'Current address'/'Permanent address', AX lines 103-106/412-415) and is announced on region ENTRY, not concatenated into each field's name. The substantive claim (SR user perceives the group name and disambiguates the two blocks) holds, but the quoted announcement string is an idealization.

Citation over-reading (not outcome-affecting): the H71 quote on .md line 60-62 is verbatim (H71.html line 23), but H71 is explicitly the fieldset/legend technique ('Providing a description for groups of form controls using fieldset and legend elements'); its Tests (lines 113-116) require fieldset+legend. The quote says fieldset/legend 'is appropriate' where a group heading is needed; it does NOT actually authorize a bare <h3>+aria-labelledby as a sufficient substitute. The doc spins it as 'H71's additional heading can suffice' without a fieldset. Because techniques are sufficient-not-necessary and 3.3.2 is met on its own merits, the passed outcome is unaffected.

Persona/scenario framing is partly self-undermining for the stated locale: the doc calls DD/MM/YYYY 'a genuinely out-of-customary format for some users' and the citation leans on 'out of the customary formats', yet for an en-GB UK government (HMRC) audience DD/MM/YYYY IS the customary date format. The 'failed' verdict therefore should not rest on non-customary format; it holds on the two-digit/four-digit specificity + the undue-navigation/visible-on-focus argument. Worth tightening the rationale, but not disqualifying.

The GDS three-box pattern (separate Day/Month/Year inputs, each labelled, confirmed in AX tree as 'Date of birth Day', 'Month', 'Year') inherently communicates field order and which value goes where, which weakens the 'instruction is strictly required' premise somewhat; the residual undisclosed detail is really only the 2-digit/4-digit digit-count expectation. The case survives this but the margin is narrower than the doc implies.

Minor: the .md 'Exact accessibility mechanism' invokes the Trusted Tester rule that the instruction must be 'visible when the form field has focus'. Contrast figure misstated: HTML comment (line 31, 88) and .md (lines 8, 52) claim ~1.3:1, but the computed contrast of #cdd4da on #fff is 1.50:1 (verified by both my own WCAG-formula calc and the inspect tool's effectiveAncestorBg). SC-attribution is contestable, not a clean 3.3.2 failure. The Member ID field DOES carry a visible, legible <label> ('Member ID' — confirmed as a LabelText/StaticText node in the AX tree). 3.3.2 is satisfied by a label OR an instruction, and the Trusted Tester 5.A test (the case's own 3rd citation) is strictly 'is a visible label/instruction present?'. A strict ACT/TT evaluator could mark this field PASSED for 3.3.2 (label present) and route the orphaned format-hint to 1.4.3. The 'failed' verdict rests on the softer intent-level reading (non-obvious format => a format instruction is needed and is not perceivable). That reading is legitimate and well-cited, but the doc overstates it as a clean normative failure.

Heavy overlap with an auto-detectable SC. axe-core/Lighthouse WILL flag the 9px / 1.50:1 instruction span as a 1.4.3 contrast violation (no incidental/disabled exemption applies; the span is visibility:visible, opacity:1, has real text). So the underlying perceptual barrier is NOT human-judgment-only — only the inference 'this unreadable text is the field's required-format instruction, so 3.3.2 is the SC that fails' requires human judgment. This dents the case's value as a pure 3.3.2 human-judgment specimen.

Boundary/contestability note (not a defect, but worth flagging): under a strict Trusted Tester 5.A reading the instruction IS present and visible on the page (sc-3.3.2 ref line 26/28: TT 5.A tests only whether a visible label/instruction is *present*, regardless of position/accuracy), and the Understanding doc explicitly permits making instructions available only on focus (lines 30-33). So a literal/normative evaluator could plausibly mark this 'passed'. The 'failed' verdict is defensible but rests on the SC's *intent* level (no undue navigation / point-of-entry exposure / no back-tracking) rather than a clear-cut normative miss. It is the most contestable form of orphaning in this folder vs. e.g. case-02 (collapsed <details>) or case-03 (9px near-background grey), which more unambiguously fail.

The instruction is not programmatically associated with #tin (no aria-describedby) and is not exposed on focus, which strengthens the intent-level fail; but this also means the harm is purely positional/visual reading-order, which is exactly the human-judgment surface the corpus wants (correctly classified).

PROMPT/FILE MISMATCH (metadata defect, not a page defect): the review prompt's Claimed scenario, selector, mechanism, and citation describe a DIFFERENT case — a 'Meridian Credit Union / Link an external bank account' two-column CSS GRID with a Routing-number hint ('9-digit number printed in the bottom-left of your check'), #routing, #nickname, and a '.hint paragraph' selector.
